title: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open Bank 2 Sensor 1
plain: The engine computer can't properly control the front air-fuel ratio sensor positive current control circuit (bank 2 sensor 1), which helps the computer run the wide-range front oxygen sensor. It sees an open or broken circuit, often from wiring, a connector or the part itself.

causes.name: Failed front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor
Blown fuse or bad relay feeding the circuit

checks: Inspect the front O2 sensor connector and wiring
Check for power at the connector and measure the part's resistance
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor.

title: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low Bank 2 Sensor 1
plain: The control circuit for the front air-fuel ratio sensor positive current control circuit (bank 2 sensor 1) is reading low voltage. This part helps the computer run the wide-range front oxygen sensor. A wire shorted to ground or a shorted part is the usual reason.

causes.name: Internally shorted front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor

checks: Check the front O2 sensor wiring for rubbed-through insulation
Measure the front O2 sensor resistance and compare with spec
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor.

title: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High Bank 2 Sensor 1
plain: The control circuit for the front air-fuel ratio sensor positive current control circuit (bank 2 sensor 1) is reading high voltage. This part helps the computer run the wide-range front oxygen sensor. A wire shorted to power, an open circuit or a failed part is the usual reason.

causes.name: Failed front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor
Control wire shorted to a power source

checks: Check the front O2 sensor wiring for shorts to other wires
Measure the front O2 sensor resistance and compare with spec
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor.

title: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open Bank 1 Sensor 1
plain: The engine computer has found a problem in the circuit for the front air-fuel ratio sensor reference voltage circuit (bank 1 sensor 1), which helps the computer run the wide-range front oxygen sensor. It usually points to wiring, a connector or the sensor itself.

causes.name: Faulty front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor

checks: Inspect the front O2 sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion
Check the sensor power, ground and signal with a meter
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor.

title: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
plain: The front air-fuel ratio sensor reference voltage circuit (bank 1 sensor 1) is giving readings that don't make sense compared with what the computer expects. This sensor helps the computer run the wide-range front oxygen sensor. The sensor may be failing or the system it watches may have a real problem.

causes.name: Failing or out-of-calibration front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor
A real fault in the system the sensor monitors
High resistance in the wiring or connector

checks: Compare the front O2 sensor reading with related sensors in live data
Check wiring and connector for corrosion or looseness
fix: Confirm the system itself is working, then replace the front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor if its readings are off.

title: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low Bank 1 Sensor 1
plain: The signal from the front air-fuel ratio sensor reference voltage circuit (bank 1 sensor 1) is lower than the computer expects. This sensor helps the computer run the wide-range front oxygen sensor. A wire shorted to ground or a failed sensor is the usual reason.

causes.name: Signal or reference wire shorted to ground
Failed front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor

checks: Inspect the front O2 sensor wiring for rubbed-through or pinched spots
Unplug the sensor and see if the reading changes, which helps separate wiring from sensor
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor.

title: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High Bank 1 Sensor 1
plain: The signal from the front air-fuel ratio sensor reference voltage circuit (bank 1 sensor 1) is higher than the computer expects. This sensor helps the computer run the wide-range front oxygen sensor. An open (broken) wire, a bad ground or a failed sensor is the usual reason.

Failed front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor

Check the sensor ground and signal wire for an open circuit
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the front air-fuel ratio (wide-band O2) sensor.

title: Secondary Air Injection System Control "A" Circuit Low
plain: The control circuit for the secondary air injection pump relay ("A") is reading low voltage. This part switches the pump that blows fresh air into the exhaust during cold starts to help the converter warm up. A wire shorted to ground or a shorted part is the usual reason.
symptoms: Usually no change in how the car drives

causes.name: Internally shorted secondary air pump relay or pump

checks: Check the secondary air relay wiring for rubbed-through insulation
Measure the secondary air relay resistance and compare with spec
fix: Repair any wiring fault first; if the wiring tests good, replace the secondary air pump relay or pump.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve - Mechanical
plain: The valve that lets boost pressure escape when you lift off the gas (bypass or diverter valve) isn't working right mechanically. Boost may leak away or the turbo may flutter.
symptoms: Loss of power or slow boost build-up
Fluttering or whooshing sound when lifting off the gas

causes.name: Torn diaphragm or worn piston in the bypass (diverter) valve
Cracked or disconnected vacuum line to the valve
Boost leak in the intake piping

checks: Inspect the bypass valve for a torn diaphragm
Check vacuum and boost hoses for cracks or loose clamps
fix: Replace the worn bypass (diverter) valve and any cracked hoses.
examples: Well known on Volkswagen and Audi 1.8T and 2.0T turbo engines

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Pressure Not Detected - Mechanical
plain: The computer expected the turbo or supercharger to build boost pressure but didn't see any. There may be a big boost leak, a failed turbo or a sensor problem.

causes.name: Large boost leak (disconnected or split intercooler hose)
Faulty boost pressure sensor or its hose
Wastegate or boost control solenoid fault

checks: Inspect all boost hoses and intercooler connections
Compare boost pressure readings with what is commanded
fix: Repair boost leaks or wastegate faults; replace the turbo only if testing shows it has failed.

cost.job: Replace boost hose or intercooler pipe

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost System Performance
plain: The turbo or supercharger isn't making the boost pressure the computer expects. Leaks, a sticking wastegate or turbo wear are typical reasons.
symptoms: Loss of power, especially when accelerating

causes.name: Boost leak from a cracked hose or loose clamp
Clogged air filter or exhaust restriction

checks: Smoke- or pressure-test the intake for boost leaks
Check wastegate or vane movement
Compare actual and desired boost in live data
fix: Fix leaks and sticking wastegate or vane controls first; replace the turbo only if it is worn out.

cost.job: Repair boost leak or replace boost control solenoid

title: Water in Fuel Sensor Circuit
plain: The engine computer has found a problem in the circuit for the water-in-fuel sensor, which warns you when water collects in the diesel fuel filter. It usually points to wiring, a connector or the sensor itself.
symptoms: Water-in-fuel warning may stay on or not work
checks: Inspect the water-in-fuel sensor connector and wiring for damage or corrosion
Check the sensor power, ground and signal with a meter
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the water-in-fuel sensor.

fix: Confirm the system itself is working, then replace the water-in-fuel sensor if its readings are off.

fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the water-in-fuel sensor.

title: Water in Fuel Sensor Circuit Intermittent
plain: The signal from the water-in-fuel sensor keeps dropping out or jumping around. This sensor warns you when water collects in the diesel fuel filter. A loose connection or a damaged wire is the usual reason.
symptoms: Water-in-fuel warning may stay on or not work

causes.name: Chafed wire that opens or shorts as the engine moves

checks: Wiggle the harness and connector while watching live data for dropouts
Inspect the water-in-fuel sensor wiring along its whole route
fix: Repair any damaged wiring or connector first; if the circuit tests good, replace the water-in-fuel sensor.

title: Water in Fuel Condition
plain: The water-in-fuel sensor has detected water in the diesel fuel filter or separator. Water can damage high-pressure fuel parts, so it should be drained soon.
symptoms: Possible rough running or loss of power

causes.name: Water collected in the fuel filter or separator
Contaminated fuel from a bad fill-up
Water entering the tank through a bad seal or cap

checks: Drain the fuel water separator
Replace the fuel filter if the code comes back
fix: Drain the water separator and replace the fuel filter; check the sensor if the light stays on with no water.

title: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean Bank 1 Sensor 2
plain: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter (bank 1, sensor 2) keeps reading lean and doesn't respond the way it should. The sensor may be worn or there may be a leak in the exhaust.
symptoms: Usually no change in how the car drives

causes.name: Worn or failed downstream oxygen sensor
Engine running lean (vacuum leak or low fuel pressure)

checks: Check for exhaust leaks around the sensor
Watch the sensor reading respond when the engine is briefly forced rich
Check front O2 sensor and fuel trims for a real lean condition
fix: Fix any exhaust leak or fuel problem; if the sensor still doesn't respond, replace it.

title: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 3 / Bank 2 Sensor 3
plain: The computer thinks the bank 1 and bank 2 sensor 3 oxygen sensors are plugged into each other's connectors. This usually happens after sensor replacement.
symptoms: Usually no change in how the car drives

causes.name: Oxygen sensor connectors plugged into the wrong side

checks: Check that each sensor's connector goes to the correct bank
Review any recent exhaust or sensor work
fix: Swap the connectors to the correct sides and clear the code.

title: Intake Air System Leak
plain: The computer has found that air is getting into the engine without being measured, which usually means a vacuum or intake leak. This makes the engine run lean.
symptoms: Hissing sound from the engine bay

causes.name: Loose or cracked air intake duct after the MAF sensor

checks: Listen for hissing at idle and inspect vacuum hoses
Smoke-test the intake system for leaks
Check that intake duct clamps are tight
fix: Find and repair the leaking hose, gasket or duct.

cost.job: Find and repair intake air leak
